transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I'm here because I've been struggling with really severe, extreme mood swings. I went through about five months of feeling completely depressed, empty, and exhausted, but over the last two months, I suddenly switched to feeling extremely energetic, hyperactive, and restless. I just don't know how to handle these intense shifts.

During this period of feeling extremely energetic and restless, did you ever have symptoms like needing very little sleep, feeling unusually powerful or invincible, or doing things that caused serious problems at work, with money, or with other people?

No, I haven't really experienced those specific symptoms. I didn't feel invincible or notice myself needing less sleep, and I haven't had any major financial or work trouble during that energetic time.

During that energetic period, did you still feel in control and able to function normally, or did it become so intense that others noticed you were clearly different, had to be hospitalized, or lost touch with reality?

People around me definitely noticed a huge difference because I was constantly moving and talking incredibly fast. I didn't lose touch with reality or need to go to the hospital, but it was very obvious to everyone that I wasn't acting like my normal self.
Did that energetic period ever cause you to become so impaired that you could not function at work, in relationships, or in daily life, even if you did not need hospitalization?
To be honest, I'm not quite sure. I haven't really thought about it that way, since I was just so focused on how much energy I suddenly had.
During that energetic period, did it interfere with your work, relationships, or daily responsibilities enough that other people were worried you could not function normally?

I'm really not sure about that. I haven't thought much about how it looked to others, since I was just so caught up in all that energy. I don't really know if they were actually worried about my ability to function.
Did you ever have a period of at least one week of this elevated or irritable energy that was severe enough to clearly change your behavior, even if you did not need hospitalization?

Yes, I definitely had that kind of elevated and irritable energy, and it lasted for about two months. My behavior was completely different during that time because I felt constantly on the go and would get easily angered by the smallest things.
During that time, did the elevated energy ever become severe enough that you needed hospitalization or had psychosis, like hallucinations or delusions?
No, I have never been hospitalized during those times. I also didn't experience any hallucinations, delusions, or anything like that.
Did that energetic period ever cause you to become so impaired that you could not function at work, in relationships, or in daily life, even if you did not need hospitalization?

I'm honestly not quite sure about that. I haven't really thought about whether it caused that level of impairment in my daily life or work. I was just so caught up in the constant need to keep moving.
Did it interfere with your work, relationships, or daily responsibilities enough that other people were worried you could not function normally?
I don't think it interfered to the point where people were worried about my ability to function. I'm not entirely sure, but no one ever expressed that kind of concern to me.
Did you ever have a period of at least one week of this elevated or irritable energy that was severe enough to clearly change your behavior, even if you did not need hospitalization?

Yes, I definitely had that kind of elevated and irritable energy, and it lasted much longer than a week—it actually went on for about two months. My behavior changed completely because I had this overflowing energy where I just couldn't sit still and kept starting multiple activities at once.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a clear manic episode lasting about 2 months with markedly elevated/irritable mood, increased energy, pressured/rapid speech, restlessness, and increased goal-directed activity noticeable to others. Although he denies psychosis, hospitalization, decreased need for sleep, or clear severe impairment, the duration and behavioral change are most consistent with mania rather than hypomania, supporting Bipolar I Disorder over Bipolar II Disorder.
